name: Concept true/false (or multiple-choice) with one-to-three-sentence justification
identify_givens: A battery of short standalone statements (typically 5-6 for the E-level Part 1) each making one claim about a security concept, mechanism or attack - e.g. equating two notions ('Privacy is a synonym for confidentiality'), attributing a mechanism ('A packet filtering firewall filters out specific content'), or naming a design principle ('...goes against the principle of economy of mechanism'). Variant: multiple-choice options A-D marked with the club symbol where zero, one or several options may be true and 'None of these answers are correct' is offered.
identify_target: For each statement, decide true/false (or mark all true options) and justify the verdict in one to three sentences by naming the correct property, definition or principle and giving the key distinction or counterexample. Grading typically awards the point if the reasoning makes at least one of the listed correct points.
identify_keywords: classify them as true or false and explain your reasoning
None of these answers are correct
strategy_name: Name the concept, then give the distinguishing counterexample

algorithm.detail: Identify which single course concept the statement tests (CIA property, firewall type, IDS class, design principle, authentication factor, salt purpose, etc.) and restate the exact assertion it makes: a definition, a mechanism, an equivalence ('synonym'), or an attribution to a named principle.

Write down (mentally) the precise course definition of that concept: e.g. packet-filtering firewall = drop whole packets based on header metadata only, never payload content; economy of mechanism = keep the security mechanism as simple and small as necessary; least privilege = grant only the access rights needed for the task.

Check the usual mismatch patterns: absolute quantifiers ('only', 'all', 'never', 'necessarily'), claimed synonyms/equivalences between notions of different scope (privacy vs confidentiality), swapped CIA properties (a read violation is confidentiality, not integrity), a real bad practice paired with the wrong named principle, or a mechanism attributed to the wrong layer (content filtering needs deep packet inspection, not packet filtering).

Mark True only if the statement is correct as written, including the named principle and quantifiers; a statement whose underlying observation is right but whose justification names the wrong principle is False. For club-marked multiple-choice, judge each option A-D independently and remember several (or none) may be true.

In 1-3 sentences: state the verdict, give the correct definition, and name the distinguishing counterexample or correction - e.g. 'False: students only need read access to most pages, so this violates least privilege; economy of mechanism means the mechanism should not be more complex than necessary.' Aim to hit at least one of the grading scheme's accepted points.

variations.name: Single T/F battery with reasoning (2022 style)
variations.detail: Six independent statements, each must be classified and justified; grading instructions accept any one of several listed correct points, so give the sharpest distinction rather than an essay. Trap: statements 2 and 5 in 2022 are false because of the mechanism/principle named, not because the intuition is wrong.

variations.name: Multiple-true club format (dasak19 Part I)
variations.detail: Options A-D under a topic header (Concepts/CIA, Authentication, Cryptography, Memory safety, Malware, IDS/Firewalls) are graded individually; zero, one or several may be true (e.g. Q9 on IDS/firewalls has A, B and C all true: signature IDS detects only known intrusions, firewalls do not stop internal threats, detection necessarily has false positives/negatives). 'None of these answers are correct' exists to separate 'all false' from 'unanswered' - never select it together with another option.

variations.name: Wrong-principle pairing trap
variations.detail: The statement describes a genuine security mistake but attributes it to the wrong Saltzer-Schroeder principle (economy of mechanism instead of least privilege, or vice versa). The algorithm adapts by verifying the named principle's definition, not just whether the practice is bad.

variations.name: Synonym/quantifier trap
variations.detail: Words like 'synonym', 'only', 'necessarily', 'never' make a roughly-true statement false: privacy is broader than confidentiality (metadata, control, context); message authentication does not require encryption of the content (only the digest is signed). Adapt step 3 to test edge cases against the quantifier.

example_problem: 2022 Part 1 T/F statement 5: 'Allowing students write access to all canvas pages in a course goes against the principle of economy of mechanism.' Classify the statement as true or false and explain your reasoning.

example_steps.work: The statement tests the Saltzer-Schroeder design principles; the claim is that granting all students write access to every Canvas page violates economy of mechanism specifically.

Recall definitions: economy of mechanism = a security mechanism should not be more complex than necessary (keep the design simple and small); least privilege = every subject should get only the access rights it needs for its tasks.

Trap found: wrong-principle pairing. Giving students write access everywhere is indeed bad practice, but the principle it offends is least privilege - students only need read access to most pages unless a task requires writing. It has nothing to do with mechanism complexity.
Verdict: False. The named principle is wrong even though the underlying permission assignment is excessive.

Justification (official solution): 'False. 1) It goes against the principle of least privilege as they only need read access to most pages unless a task requires them to write. 2) Economy of mechanism means that a security mechanism should not be more complex than necessary.' Making at least one of these two points earns the mark.
